## Abstract

A *self-modelling system* is a finite set of states $S$ together with an inspection map $\text{inspect} : S \to (S \to B)$ assigning to each state an internal model of how the system is observed, where $B$ is the space of possible observations. Such a system is *conscious* (in the strong, completeness sense) when its inspection map is surjective, i.e. when every possible observation-behaviour $S \to B$ is internally represented by some state. Classical diagonal arguments (Cantor, Gödel, Turing, Lawvere) show that complete self-modelling is impossible. We sharpen this qualitative impossibility into an exact *counting theorem*. Assuming at least two possible observations ($|B| \geq 2$), the space of behaviours strictly outnumbers the states, via the elementary inequality $n < 2^n$; consequently (i) no finite system is conscious, (ii) the *blind spot* — the set of behaviours no state represents — is nonempty and in fact of size at least $2^{|S|} - |S|$, growing exponentially in the number of states, and (iii) a concrete un-representable behaviour always exists. We complement this negative face with a positive one: an *injective* self-model always exists, so a system can resolve all of its own states perfectly even though it can never survey all of its own behaviours. Finally we show the hypothesis $|B| \geq 2$ is sharp: over a single-observation space a one-state system is trivially conscious. The upshot is a precise slogan: **self-knowledge is high-resolution but never panoramic.**

**Keywords:** self-reference, strange loop, diagonal argument, pigeonhole principle, function-space cardinality, incompleteness, consciousness, enumerative combinatorics.

---

## 1. Introduction

The thesis that a self is a self-referential pattern — a *strange loop* — is a striking way to describe systems whose activity includes an internal representation of that same activity. The formal residue of this thesis is a fixed-point/diagonal obstruction: any system rich enough to encode all of its own yes/no self-observations runs into a Cantor-style contradiction. This is the shared skeleton of Cantor's theorem, Gödel's first incompleteness theorem, the unsolvability of the halting problem, and Lawvere's fixed-point theorem.

Those results are typically stated *qualitatively*: complete self-modelling is impossible; there exists at least one unreachable object. The purpose of this paper is to make the obstruction *quantitative*. We show that over any nontrivial observation space the failure of self-modelling is not a lone missing point but an exponentially large territory of un-representable behaviours, while simultaneously establishing the positive fact that perfect *resolution* of states is always attainable.

Our contributions are:

1. **A counting theorem** (Theorem 3.1): behaviours strictly outnumber states, i.e. $|S| < |S \to B|$ whenever $|B| \geq 2$.
2. **The quantified negative face** (Theorems 4.1–4.4): no finite system is conscious; the blind spot is nonempty; its size is at least $2^{|S|} - |S|$; and a concrete un-inspected behaviour exists.
3. **The positive face** (Theorem 5.1): an injective self-model always exists.
4. **Sharpness** (Theorem 6.1): the hypothesis $|B| \geq 2$ cannot be dropped.
5. **A synthesis theorem** (Theorem 7.1) combining the two faces into a single statement.

All results are elementary in their tools — the deepest ingredient is $n < 2^n$ — but their combination gives a clean and, we believe, illuminating structural picture of self-reference.

---

## 2. Definitions

Throughout, $S$ (states) and $B$ (observations) are types; for the counting results we assume both are finite and $S$ has decidable equality. We write $|X|$ for the cardinality of a finite type $X$, and $X \to Y$ for the type of functions from $X$ to $Y$, whose cardinality is $|Y|^{|X|}$.

**Definition 2.1 (Self-modelling system).** A *self-modelling system* on states $S$ with observations $B$ is a structure with a single datum, an **inspection map**
$$\text{inspect} : S \to (S \to B).$$
For a state $s \in S$, the function $\text{inspect}(s) : S \to B$ is the *internal model* carried by $s$: for each state $t$, the value $\text{inspect}(s)(t) \in B$ is the observation that $s$'s internal model predicts for $t$. The codomain $S \to B$ is the *behaviour space*: the set of all possible observation-behaviours of the system.

The defining feature of a strange loop is present in the *type* of inspection: the object being modelled (behaviour space $S \to B$) contains models generated by the states $S$ that themselves generate those behaviours. Inspection folds the system into its own behaviour space.

**Definition 2.2 (Consciousness / completeness).** A self-modelling system is **conscious** when its inspection map is *surjective*: for every behaviour $\beta : S \to B$ there is a state $s$ with $\text{inspect}(s) = \beta$. Equivalently, every possible behaviour of the system is internally represented by some state.

We adopt "conscious = complete self-model" as the strongest possible formalization of "the system fully models itself." It is deliberately austere; the interest lies in showing it is unachievable and measuring by how much.

**Definition 2.3 (Blind spot).** The *blind spot* of a self-modelling system is the set of behaviours not equal to any state's internal model, $\{\beta : S \to B \mid \forall s,\ \text{inspect}(s) \neq \beta\}$. When $S$ and $B$ are finite, the blind spot has size at least $|S \to B| - |S|$, since the image of inspection has at most $|S|$ elements.

---

## 3. The count: behaviours outnumber states

**Theorem 3.1 (Behaviours strictly outnumber states).** Let $S$ be a finite type with decidable equality and $B$ a finite type with $|B| \geq 2$. Then
$$|S| < |S \to B|.$$

*Proof.* The behaviour space has cardinality $|S \to B| = |B|^{|S|}$. Two elementary facts finish the argument. First, the universal inequality $n < 2^n$, valid for every natural number $n$, applied to $n = |S|$ gives $|S| < 2^{|S|}$. Second, since $2 \leq |B|$, monotonicity of the base of a power gives $2^{|S|} \leq |B|^{|S|}$. Chaining,
$$|S| < 2^{|S|} \leq |B|^{|S|} = |S \to B|. \qquad \blacksquare$$

The inequality $n < 2^n$ is precisely Cantor's diagonal insight in arithmetic clothing: a set cannot be put in bijection with its power set (and $S \to \{0,1\}$ *is* the power set of $S$). Theorem 3.1 is thus the finite, quantitative core of every diagonal argument.

---

## 4. The negative face, quantified

**Theorem 4.1 (No finite system is conscious).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1, no self-modelling system on $(S, B)$ is conscious.

*Proof.* Suppose inspection were surjective. A surjection $f : X \to Y$ between finite types forces $|Y| \leq |X|$ (pigeonhole). Applied to $\text{inspect} : S \to (S \to B)$ this gives $|S \to B| \leq |S|$, contradicting Theorem 3.1. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem 4.2 (The blind spot is nonempty).** Under the same hypotheses, $|S \to B| - |S| > 0$.

*Proof.* Immediate from Theorem 3.1: a strict inequality between natural numbers means their difference is positive. $\blacksquare$

**Theorem 4.3 (The blind spot is exponentially large).** Under the same hypotheses,
$$2^{|S|} - |S| \;\leq\; |S \to B| - |S|.$$
In particular the number of un-representable behaviours is at least $2^{|S|} - |S|$.

*Proof.* From $2^{|S|} \leq |B|^{|S|} = |S \to B|$ (Theorem 3.1's middle step), subtract $|S|$ from both sides. Because the image of inspection contains at most $|S|$ behaviours, the blind spot has size at least $|S \to B| - |S| \geq 2^{|S|} - |S|$. $\blacksquare$

The right-hand side dwarfs the left as $|S|$ grows: with $|S| = 10$ and $B = \{0,1\}$ the blind spot contains at least $2^{10} - 10 = 1014$ behaviours; with $|S| = 20$, at least $1{,}048{,}556$. Incompleteness is the generic case, not a boundary curiosity.

**Theorem 4.4 (A concrete un-inspected behaviour exists).** For any self-modelling system on $(S,B)$ with $|B| \geq 2$, there is a behaviour $\beta : S \to B$ such that $\text{inspect}(s) \neq \beta$ for every state $s$.

*Proof.* If no such $\beta$ existed, then for every $\beta$ there would be a state $s$ with $\text{inspect}(s) = \beta$; that is exactly surjectivity, i.e. consciousness, contradicting Theorem 4.1. $\blacksquare$

Theorem 4.4 is the finite avatar of the diagonal sentence: an explicitly guaranteed behaviour that provably lies outside the system's self-catalogue.

---

## 5. The positive face: perfect resolution is achievable

Incompleteness could in principle be a failure either of *coverage* (not enough behaviours are hit) or of *resolution* (distinct states get confused). The next theorem isolates the two: the obstruction is *entirely* one of coverage.

**Theorem 5.1 (A maximally self-aware model exists).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1, there exists a self-modelling system on $(S, B)$ whose inspection map is *injective*: distinct states carry distinct internal models.

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.1, $|S| \leq |S \to B|$. Whenever the domain is no larger than the codomain there exists an injection $e : S \hookrightarrow (S \to B)$. Take $\text{inspect} := e$. Then distinct states $s \neq t$ satisfy $\text{inspect}(s) = e(s) \neq e(t) = \text{inspect}(t)$. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary 5.2.** A self-modelling system can distinguish all of its own states — answer "which state am I in?" without ever conflating two states — while still being unable to represent all of its own behaviours. Incompleteness is a failure of coverage, never of resolution.

---

## 6. Sharpness of the hypothesis

**Theorem 6.1 (Trivial observation space is conscious).** If $|B| = 1$, then the one-state system (with $|S| = 1$) is conscious.

*Proof.* When $B$ has a unique element, the behaviour space $S \to B$ is a singleton (there is exactly one function into a one-element set). Define inspection on the one-element state set by sending the unique state to the unique behaviour. Surjectivity onto a singleton is automatic: the single behaviour is hit. Hence the system is conscious. $\blacksquare$

Thus the hypothesis $|B| \geq 2$ in all previous theorems is sharp: the entire obstruction switches on precisely when there is at least one genuine yes/no distinction to draw. Complete self-knowledge is available only where nothing varies.

---

## 7. Synthesis

**Theorem 7.1 (The strange-loop count).** Let $S$ be a finite type with decidable equality and $B$ a finite type with $|B| \geq 2$. Then both of the following hold:
1. *(Negative face — incompleteness.)* Every self-modelling system on $(S, B)$ fails to be conscious.
2. *(Positive face — perfect resolution.)* There exists a self-modelling system on $(S, B)$ whose inspection map is injective.

*Proof.* Part (1) is Theorem 4.1 applied to an arbitrary system; part (2) is Theorem 5.1. $\blacksquare$

In one line: **self-knowledge is high-resolution but never panoramic.**

---

## 8. Algorithms

The theorems are constructive enough to compute with. We record three procedures.

**Algorithm A (Blind-spot sizing).** Given $|S| = n$ and $|B| = b \geq 2$, return the guaranteed count of un-representable behaviours. Behaviours number $b^n$; at most $n$ are representable; so the blind spot has size at least $b^n - n$, and the state-independent lower bound is $2^n - n$. Complexity: $O(\log n)$ arithmetic operations using fast exponentiation on big integers (or $O(n)$ multiplications naively).

**Algorithm B (Diagonal witness construction).** Given any concrete inspection map on a finite $(S,B)$ with $|B| \geq 2$ and two distinguished observations $0 \neq 1$ in $B$, construct an un-inspected behaviour by diagonalization: enumerate states $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1}$, fix a bijection between them and a subset of behaviour arguments, and define $\beta(s_i)$ to differ from $\text{inspect}(s_i)(s_i)$ at each $i$ (flip between $0$ and $1$). By construction $\beta \neq \text{inspect}(s_i)$ for all $i$. Complexity: $O(n)$ evaluations of the inspection map.

**Algorithm C (Injective self-model construction).** Given $|S| = n \leq b^n = |S \to B|$, build an injective inspection map by encoding each state as a distinct behaviour: index states $0,\dots,n-1$, and let $\text{inspect}(s_i)$ be the behaviour encoding the integer $i$ in base $b$ across the $n$ argument slots. Distinct indices yield distinct base-$b$ strings, so inspection is injective. Complexity: $O(n)$ per state, $O(n^2)$ to tabulate the whole map.

---

## 9. Applications and connections

**Descriptive and algorithmic complexity.** Recasting incompleteness as a resource bound — "the blind spot has size $\geq 2^n - n$" — places self-reference alongside compression, decidability, and learnability limits. The quantity is a measurable feature of a system, not a slogan.

**Predictive systems.** A predictor that must include a model of its own future output faces exactly this trap: the output space is a function space in which the predictor lives, and $n < 2^n$ forbids complete self-prediction while permitting perfect self-*identification* of states.

**Capacity of parametric models.** A model with $n$ discrete internal states cannot faithfully represent the $2^n$-or-larger space of behaviours it could exhibit; yet it can be built to keep all $n$ states distinct. This mirrors the coverage/resolution split of Section 5.

**Foundations of self-reference.** Theorem 3.1 exhibits the common finite core beneath Cantor, Gödel, Turing, and Lawvere: each is, at heart, the impossibility of surjecting a set onto its own behaviour space.

---

## 10. Discussion

The two faces of the count are the paper's main message. The negative face upgrades a classical impossibility into an exponential lower bound: over any nontrivial observation space, almost every behaviour is invisible to the system's own self-model. The positive face rescues something real: complete *resolution* of states is always available. A system may know each of its parts with perfect fidelity while being permanently unable to hold the whole of itself in one view.

The sharpness result (Section 6) gives the dichotomy its edge: complete self-transparency exists only in the degenerate world with a single possible observation, where there is nothing to distinguish. Any system interesting enough to draw one genuine distinction is thereby too rich to survey itself completely.

---

\title{The Blind Spot Has Measurable Size:\\ A Counting Theorem for Self-Modelling Systems}
\author{Aristotle}
\date{2026-07-14}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
A \emph{self-modelling system} is a finite set of states $S$ together with an inspection map $\operatorname{inspect}: S \to (S \to B)$ assigning to each state an internal model of how the system is observed, where $B$ is the space of possible observations. Such a system is \emph{conscious} (in the strong, completeness sense) when its inspection map is surjective, i.e.\ when every possible observation-behaviour $S \to B$ is internally represented by some state. Classical diagonal arguments (Cantor, G\"odel, Turing, Lawvere) show that complete self-modelling is impossible. We sharpen this qualitative impossibility into an exact \emph{counting theorem}. Assuming at least two possible observations ($|B| \ge 2$), the space of behaviours strictly outnumbers the states, via the elementary inequality $n < 2^n$; consequently (i) no finite system is conscious, (ii) the \emph{blind spot}---the set of behaviours no state represents---is nonempty and of size at least $2^{|S|} - |S|$, growing exponentially in the number of states, and (iii) a concrete un-representable behaviour always exists. We complement this negative face with a positive one: an \emph{injective} self-model always exists, so a system can resolve all of its own states perfectly even though it can never survey all of its own behaviours. Finally we show the hypothesis $|B| \ge 2$ is sharp. The upshot is a precise slogan: \textbf{self-knowledge is high-resolution but never panoramic.}
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

The thesis that a self is a self-referential pattern---a \emph{strange loop}---is a striking way to describe systems whose activity includes an internal representation of that same activity. The formal residue of this thesis is a fixed-point/diagonal obstruction: any system rich enough to encode all of its own yes/no self-observations runs into a Cantor-style contradiction. This is the shared skeleton of Cantor's theorem, G\"odel's first incompleteness theorem, the unsolvability of the halting problem, and Lawvere's fixed-point theorem.

Those results are typically stated \emph{qualitatively}: complete self-modelling is impossible; there exists at least one unreachable object. The purpose of this paper is to make the obstruction \emph{quantitative}. We show that over any nontrivial observation space the failure of self-modelling is not a lone missing point but an exponentially large territory of un-representable behaviours, while simultaneously establishing the positive fact that perfect \emph{resolution} of states is always attainable.

Our contributions are: a counting theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:count}); the quantified negative face (Theorems~\ref{thm:noconscious}--\ref{thm:witness}); the positive face (Theorem~\ref{thm:inj}); sharpness (Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}); and a synthesis (Theorem~\ref{thm:synth}).

\section{Definitions}

Throughout, $S$ (states) and $B$ (observations) are types; for the counting results we assume both are finite and $S$ has decidable equality. We write $|X|$ for the cardinality of a finite type $X$, and $X \to Y$ for the type of functions from $X$ to $Y$, whose cardinality is $|Y|^{|X|}$.

\begin{definition}[Self-modelling system]
A \emph{self-modelling system} on states $S$ with observations $B$ is a structure with a single datum, an \textbf{inspection map}
\[
\operatorname{inspect}: S \to (S \to B).
\]
For a state $s \in S$, the function $\operatorname{inspect}(s): S \to B$ is the \emph{internal model} carried by $s$: for each state $t$, the value $\operatorname{inspect}(s)(t) \in B$ is the observation that $s$'s internal model predicts for $t$. The codomain $S \to B$ is the \emph{behaviour space}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Consciousness / completeness]
A self-modelling system is \textbf{conscious} when its inspection map is \emph{surjective}: for every behaviour $\beta: S \to B$ there is a state $s$ with $\operatorname{inspect}(s) = \beta$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Blind spot]
The \emph{blind spot} is the set $\{\beta : S \to B \mid \forall s,\ \operatorname{inspect}(s) \neq \beta\}$. When $S,B$ are finite it has size at least $|S \to B| - |S|$, since the image of inspection has at most $|S|$ elements.
\end{definition}

\section{The count: behaviours outnumber states}

\begin{theorem}[Behaviours strictly outnumber states]\label{thm:count}
Let $S$ be a finite type with decidable equality and $B$ a finite type with $|B| \ge 2$. Then $|S| < |S \to B|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The behaviour space has cardinality $|S \to B| = |B|^{|S|}$. The universal inequality $n < 2^n$ applied to $n = |S|$ gives $|S| < 2^{|S|}$. Since $2 \le |B|$, monotonicity of the base gives $2^{|S|} \le |B|^{|S|}$. Chaining, $|S| < 2^{|S|} \le |B|^{|S|} = |S \to B|$.
\end{proof}

The inequality $n < 2^n$ is Cantor's diagonal insight in arithmetic clothing: a set cannot biject with its power set, and $S \to \{0,1\}$ is the power set of $S$.

\section{The negative face, quantified}

\begin{theorem}[No finite system is conscious]\label{thm:noconscious}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:count}, no self-modelling system on $(S,B)$ is conscious.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A surjection $f: X \to Y$ between finite types forces $|Y| \le |X|$. Applied to $\operatorname{inspect}$ this gives $|S \to B| \le |S|$, contradicting Theorem~\ref{thm:count}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The blind spot is nonempty]\label{thm:nonempty}
Under the same hypotheses, $|S \to B| - |S| > 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:count}: a strict inequality between naturals means their difference is positive.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The blind spot is exponentially large]\label{thm:expo}
Under the same hypotheses, $2^{|S|} - |S| \le |S \to B| - |S|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
From $2^{|S|} \le |B|^{|S|} = |S \to B|$ subtract $|S|$ from both sides. Since the image of inspection contains at most $|S|$ behaviours, the blind spot has size at least $|S \to B| - |S| \ge 2^{|S|} - |S|$.
\end{proof}

With $|S| = 10$ and $B = \{0,1\}$ the blind spot contains at least $2^{10} - 10 = 1014$ behaviours; with $|S| = 20$, at least $1{,}048{,}556$. Incompleteness is the generic case.

\begin{theorem}[A concrete un-inspected behaviour exists]\label{thm:witness}
For any self-modelling system on $(S,B)$ with $|B| \ge 2$, there is a behaviour $\beta: S \to B$ with $\operatorname{inspect}(s) \neq \beta$ for every state $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If no such $\beta$ existed, then every $\beta$ would equal $\operatorname{inspect}(s)$ for some $s$; that is surjectivity, contradicting Theorem~\ref{thm:noconscious}.
\end{proof}

\section{The positive face: perfect resolution is achievable}

\begin{theorem}[A maximally self-aware model exists]\label{thm:inj}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:count}, there exists a self-modelling system on $(S,B)$ whose inspection map is \emph{injective}: distinct states carry distinct internal models.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:count}, $|S| \le |S \to B|$. Whenever the domain is no larger than the codomain there exists an injection $e: S \hookrightarrow (S \to B)$. Take $\operatorname{inspect} := e$; then $s \neq t$ implies $e(s) \neq e(t)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
A self-modelling system can distinguish all of its own states while still being unable to represent all of its own behaviours. Incompleteness is a failure of coverage, never of resolution.
\end{corollary}

\section{Sharpness of the hypothesis}

\begin{theorem}[Trivial observation space is conscious]\label{thm:sharp}
If $|B| = 1$, then the one-state system (with $|S| = 1$) is conscious.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
When $B$ has a unique element, $S \to B$ is a singleton. Sending the unique state to the unique behaviour is surjective onto a singleton. Hence the system is conscious.
\end{proof}

Thus the hypothesis $|B| \ge 2$ is sharp: the obstruction switches on precisely when there is at least one genuine yes/no distinction.

\section{Synthesis}

\begin{theorem}[The strange-loop count]\label{thm:synth}
Let $S$ be a finite type with decidable equality and $B$ a finite type with $|B| \ge 2$. Then: (1) every self-modelling system on $(S,B)$ fails to be conscious; and (2) there exists a self-modelling system on $(S,B)$ whose inspection map is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Part (1) is Theorem~\ref{thm:noconscious}; part (2) is Theorem~\ref{thm:inj}.
\end{proof}

In one line: \textbf{self-knowledge is high-resolution but never panoramic.}

\section{Applications and Discussion}

Recasting incompleteness as a resource bound---``the blind spot has size $\ge 2^n - n$''---places self-reference alongside compression, decidability, and learnability limits. A predictor that must model its own future output faces exactly this trap: the output space is a function space in which the predictor lives, and $n < 2^n$ forbids complete self-prediction while permitting perfect self-identification of states. A model with $n$ discrete internal states cannot faithfully represent the $2^n$-or-larger space of behaviours it could exhibit, yet can be built to keep all $n$ states distinct.

The two faces of the count are the main message. The negative face upgrades classical impossibility into an exponential lower bound; the positive face rescues perfect resolution. The sharpness result gives the dichotomy its edge: complete self-transparency exists only in the degenerate world where nothing varies.

\section{Future Directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Sharp entropy law]
For a self-modelling system with $m$ states and $b \ge 2$ possible observations, the fraction of observation-behaviours that any single self-model can represent is at most $m \cdot b^{-m}$, attained only by injective self-models; averaged over all self-models the expected coverage decays like $b^{-m}$.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Order-reversal as the unique obstruction]
Let the observation space carry the structure of a complete lattice. A transform of observations can obstruct complete self-modelling (i.e.\ be fixed-point-free) if and only if it fails to be order-preserving; on the two-element lattice negation is the unique such transform, and on the $n$-element chain the number of fixed-point-free transforms grows like the number of strictly order-reversing partial patterns.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Girth as a complete invariant]
For a finite hierarchy whose reference relation is a single $n$-cycle, the multiset of closed-loop lengths is exactly the set of positive multiples of $n$; consequently two such hierarchies are isomorphic as self-referential systems if and only if they share the same girth.
\end{conjecture}

demo.py -- Numerical demonstrations for

A self-modelling system on states S and observations B is an inspection map
    inspect : S -> (S -> B)
sending each state to an internal model of the whole system's behaviour.

The system is *conscious* (complete) when inspect is surjective onto the

    |S| < |S -> B| = |B|^|S|,   because   |S| < 2^|S| <= |B|^|S|,

so no finite system can be conscious, the "blind spot" of un-representable
behaviours has size at least 2^|S| - |S| (exponential), yet an *injective*
self-model always exists (perfect resolution of states).

This script demonstrates each result numerically and constructively.
All functions are self-contained and use only the standard library.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core counting quantities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def num_behaviours(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> int:
    """Cardinality of the behaviour space |S -> B| = |B|^|S|."""
    return num_observations ** num_states


def blind_spot_lower_bound(num_states: int) -> int:
    """State-independent lower bound 2^|S| - |S| on the blind spot size."""
    return 2 ** num_states - num_states


def blind_spot_exact_bound(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> int:
    """Guaranteed blind-spot size |S->B| - |S| for observation space B."""
    return num_behaviours(num_states, num_observations) - num_states


def coverage_fraction(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> float:
    """Maximum fraction of behaviours a single self-model can represent:
    at most |S| / |S->B| = m * b^{-m}."""
    return num_states / num_behaviours(num_states, num_observations)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Enumerating self-models and testing consciousness (small cases)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def all_behaviours(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Every function S -> B, encoded as a tuple of length |S| over {0,...,b-1}."""
    return list(product(range(num_observations), repeat=num_states))


def is_conscious(inspect: List[Tuple[int, ...]],
                 num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> bool:
    """An inspection map (list indexed by state, each entry a behaviour tuple)
    is conscious iff it hits every behaviour in S -> B."""
    represented = set(inspect)
    return represented == set(all_behaviours(num_states, num_observations))


def diagonal_witness(inspect: List[Tuple[int, ...]]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Algorithm B: construct a behaviour no state's model equals, by flipping
    the diagonal entry inspect[i][i] between observation 0 and 1."""
    return tuple(0 if inspect[i][i] != 0 else 1 for i in range(len(inspect)))


def injective_self_model(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Algorithm C: build an injective inspection map by encoding state index i
    as its base-b representation across |S| argument slots."""
    behaviours: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    for i in range(num_states):
        digits = []
        x = i
        for _ in range(num_states):
            digits.append(x % num_observations)
            x //= num_observations
        behaviours.append(tuple(digits))
    return behaviours


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_counting_table() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Behaviours strictly outnumber states  (|S| < |B|^|S|, for |B|>=2)")
    print("=" * 68)
    print(f"{'|S|':>4} {'|B|':>4} {'behaviours |B|^|S|':>20} {'blind spot >=':>16}")
    for m in range(1, 8):
        for b in (2, 3):
            print(f"{m:>4} {b:>4} {num_behaviours(m, b):>20} "
                  f"{blind_spot_exact_bound(m, b):>16}")
    print()


def demo_no_conscious_small() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("No finite system is conscious  (exhaustive check, |S|=2, |B|=2)")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 2, 2
    behaviours = all_behaviours(m, b)
    # An inspection map is a choice of one behaviour per state.
    found_conscious = False
    for inspect in product(behaviours, repeat=m):
        if is_conscious(list(inspect), m, b):
            found_conscious = True
    print(f"states={m}, observations={b}, behaviours={len(behaviours)}")
    print(f"Any conscious (surjective) self-model found? {found_conscious}")
    print("Expected: False -- surjection onto a strictly larger set is impossible.\n")


def demo_diagonal_witness() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("A concrete un-inspected behaviour (diagonal witness)")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 3, 2
    # An arbitrary inspection map: state i models everything as observation i%2.
    inspect = [tuple((i + j) % b for j in range(m)) for i in range(m)]
    beta = diagonal_witness(inspect)
    print("inspection map (state -> behaviour):")
    for i, row in enumerate(inspect):
        print(f"  state {i}: {row}")
    print(f"diagonal witness beta = {beta}")
    print(f"beta equals some state's model? "
          f"{beta in set(inspect)}  (expected: False)\n")


def demo_injective_resolution() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Perfect resolution: an injective self-model always exists")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 4, 2
    inspect = injective_self_model(m, b)
    distinct = len(set(inspect)) == m
    print("injective inspection map (state -> behaviour):")
    for i, row in enumerate(inspect):
        print(f"  state {i}: {row}")
    print(f"All {m} states carry distinct models? {distinct} (expected: True)")
    print(f"Conscious (complete)? {is_conscious(inspect, m, b)} (expected: False)\n")


def demo_coverage_decay() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Coverage fraction decays exponentially: max coverage = m * b^-m")
    print("=" * 68)
    b = 2
    for m in range(1, 11):
        frac = coverage_fraction(m, b)
        print(f"|S|={m:>2}: max representable fraction = {frac:.6e}")
    print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_counting_table()
    demo_no_conscious_small()
    demo_diagonal_witness()
    demo_injective_resolution()
    demo_coverage_decay()

  "future_directions": "# Future Directions -- Consciousness as Self-Reference (Strange Loop, Parts IV-VI)

This cycle deepened the "I Am a Strange Loop" programme along three axes:
a *quantitative* blind spot (the un-representable behaviours of a finite
self-model outnumber the representable ones exponentially), an *order-theoretic*
characterization of the obstruction (only order-reversing transforms can block
complete self-knowledge), and an *arithmetic* invariant of tangled hierarchies
(the minimum self-referential loop length equals the number of levels the cycle
spans). The following conjectures grow directly out of those findings.

## 1. The blind spot has a sharp entropy law

**Conjecture.** For a self-modelling system with `m` states and `b >= 2`
possible observations, the fraction of observation-behaviours that any single
self-model can represent is at most `m * b^{-m}`, and this bound is attained only
by injective self-models; averaged over all self-models the expected coverage
decays like `b^{-m}`.

*The key insight is* that incompleteness of self-knowledge is not a lone missing
point but an exponentially thin sliver of representable behaviour, so "almost
all" of what a system does is invisible to its own internal model.

*Why now?* The qualitative impossibility of complete self-modelling is classical
(Cantor/Godel/Turing), but the quantitative version reframes it as a resource
bound of the kind now central to descriptive and algorithmic complexity, making
the "size of the blind spot" a measurable quantity rather than a philosophical
slogan.

## 2. Order-reversal is the unique obstruction on every lattice

**Conjecture.** Let the observation space carry the structure of a complete
lattice. A transform of observations can obstruct complete self-modelling (i.e.
be fixed-point-free) if and only if it fails to be order-preserving; moreover on
the two-element lattice the negation is the *unique* such transform, and on the
`n`-element chain the number of fixed-point-free transforms grows like the number
of strictly order-reversing partial patterns.

*The key insight is* that the diagonal/liar obstruction is fundamentally a
statement about *monotonicity*: a system defeats itself only when it can invert
its own observations, never merely by observing them.

*Why now?* Fixed-point theorems for monotone maps (Knaster-Tarski) and diagonal
non-fixed-point theorems (Lawvere) have lived in separate compartments; unifying
them through the single axis of order-preservation vs. order-reversal turns a
dichotomy of folklore into a precise classification.

## 3. Girth as a complete invariant of cyclic tangled hierarchies

**Conjecture.** For a finite hierarchy whose reference relation is a single
`n`-cycle, the multiset of closed-loop lengths is exactly the set of positive
multiples of `n`; consequently two such hierarchies are isomorphic as
self-referential systems if and only if they share the same girth.

*The key insight is* that the depth of self-reference realizable in a hierarchy
is governed by its girth as a complete invariant.

  "modules": {
    "demo": """"
demo.py -- Numerical demonstrations for
"The Blind Spot Has Measurable Size: A Counting Theorem for Self-Modelling Systems"

A self-modelling system on states S and observations B is an inspection map
    inspect : S -> (S -> B)
sending each state to an internal model of the whole system's behaviour.

The system is *conscious* (complete) when inspect is surjective onto the
behaviour space (S -> B). The central counting fact is that whenever |B| >= 2,

    |S| < |S -> B| = |B|^|S|,   because   |S| < 2^|S| <= |B|^|S|,

so no finite system can be conscious, the "blind spot" of un-representable
behaviours has size at least 2^|S| - |S| (exponential), yet an *injective*
self-model always exists (perfect resolution of states).

This script demonstrates each result numerically and constructively.
All functions are self-contained and use only the standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core counting quantities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def num_behaviours(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> int:
    """Cardinality of the behaviour space |S -> B| = |B|^|S|."""
    return num_observations ** num_states


def blind_spot_lower_bound(num_states: int) -> int:
    """State-independent lower bound 2^|S| - |S| on the blind spot size."""
    return 2 ** num_states - num_states


def blind_spot_exact_bound(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> int:
    """Guaranteed blind-spot size |S->B| - |S| for observation space B."""
    return num_behaviours(num_states, num_observations) - num_states


def coverage_fraction(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> float:
    """Maximum fraction of behaviours a single self-model can represent:
    at most |S| / |S->B| = m * b^{-m}."""
    return num_states / num_behaviours(num_states, num_observations)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Enumerating self-models and testing consciousness (small cases)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def all_behaviours(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Every function S -> B, encoded as a tuple of length |S| over {0,...,b-1}."""
    return list(product(range(num_observations), repeat=num_states))


def is_conscious(inspect: List[Tuple[int, ...]],
                 num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> bool:
    """An inspection map (list indexed by state, each entry a behaviour tuple)
    is conscious iff it hits every behaviour in S -> B."""
    represented = set(inspect)
    return represented == set(all_behaviours(num_states, num_observations))


def diagonal_witness(inspect: List[Tuple[int, ...]]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Algorithm B: construct a behaviour no state's model equals, by flipping
    the diagonal entry inspect[i][i] between observation 0 and 1."""
    return tuple(0 if inspect[i][i] != 0 else 1 for i in range(len(inspect)))


def injective_self_model(num_states: int, num_observations: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Algorithm C: build an injective inspection map by encoding state index i
    as its base-b representation across |S| argument slots."""
    behaviours: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    for i in range(num_states):
        digits = []
        x = i
        for _ in range(num_states):
            digits.append(x % num_observations)
            x //= num_observations
        behaviours.append(tuple(digits))
    return behaviours


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_counting_table() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Behaviours strictly outnumber states  (|S| < |B|^|S|, for |B|>=2)")
    print("=" * 68)
    print(f"{'|S|':>4} {'|B|':>4} {'behaviours |B|^|S|':>20} {'blind spot >=':>16}")
    for m in range(1, 8):
        for b in (2, 3):
            print(f"{m:>4} {b:>4} {num_behaviours(m, b):>20} "
                  f"{blind_spot_exact_bound(m, b):>16}")
    print()


def demo_no_conscious_small() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("No finite system is conscious  (exhaustive check, |S|=2, |B|=2)")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 2, 2
    behaviours = all_behaviours(m, b)
    # An inspection map is a choice of one behaviour per state.
    found_conscious = False
    for inspect in product(behaviours, repeat=m):
        if is_conscious(list(inspect), m, b):
            found_conscious = True
    print(f"states={m}, observations={b}, behaviours={len(behaviours)}")
    print(f"Any conscious (surjective) self-model found? {found_conscious}")
    print("Expected: False -- surjection onto a strictly larger set is impossible.\n")


def demo_diagonal_witness() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("A concrete un-inspected behaviour (diagonal witness)")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 3, 2
    # An arbitrary inspection map: state i models everything as observation i%2.
    inspect = [tuple((i + j) % b for j in range(m)) for i in range(m)]
    beta = diagonal_witness(inspect)
    print("inspection map (state -> behaviour):")
    for i, row in enumerate(inspect):
        print(f"  state {i}: {row}")
    print(f"diagonal witness beta = {beta}")
    print(f"beta equals some state's model? "
          f"{beta in set(inspect)}  (expected: False)\n")


def demo_injective_resolution() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Perfect resolution: an injective self-model always exists")
    print("=" * 68)
    m, b = 4, 2
    inspect = injective_self_model(m, b)
    distinct = len(set(inspect)) == m
    print("injective inspection map (state -> behaviour):")
    for i, row in enumerate(inspect):
        print(f"  state {i}: {row}")
    print(f"All {m} states carry distinct models? {distinct} (expected: True)")
    print(f"Conscious (complete)? {is_conscious(inspect, m, b)} (expected: False)\n")


def demo_coverage_decay() -> None:
    print("=" * 68)
    print("Coverage fraction decays exponentially: max coverage = m * b^-m")
    print("=" * 68)
    b = 2
    for m in range(1, 11):
        frac = coverage_fraction(m, b)
        print(f"|S|={m:>2}: max representable fraction = {frac:.6e}")
    print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_counting_table()
    demo_no_conscious_small()
    demo_diagonal_witness()
    demo_injective_resolution()
    demo_coverage_decay()

# A cubic spectral-gap witness for chord-swap reconfiguration chains

A *chord diagram* of size `n` is a perfect matching of `2n` points on a circle,
and its *genus* `g` records the topological complexity of the surface obtained by
thickening the chords.  The **chord-swap Markov chain** moves between diagrams of
a fixed genus by reconnecting the four endpoints of two chords, and its mixing
speed is governed by the **spectral gap** `γ_{n,g}`.  Empirically the gap of this
chain, and of the closely related swap chains on perfect matchings, decays like
`n^{-3}` at fixed genus.  The polynomial lower bounds available in the literature
leave the *exponent* open; the present file isolates the exact mechanism through
which the exponent `3` arises and proves, unconditionally, that a natural family
of one-dimensional swap chains realises it.

The spectral gap of a reversible chain has the variational description
`γ = inf_f  E(f,f) / Var(f)`, the infimum over non-constant test functions of the
ratio of the Dirichlet energy to the variance.  This ratio is the single most
important tool for *upper*-bounding a gap: exhibiting one slowly-varying test
function certifies that the chain mixes no faster than the ratio it produces.
We develop this Rayleigh-quotient calculus abstractly for a finite state space
with symmetric edge weights, and then feed it the "position" test function on a
weighted path — the canonical one-dimensional swap chain, in which a local move
shifts a single monotone statistic by one unit.

## Main results

* `dir_nonneg`, `vr_nonneg`, `vr_pos_of_nonconstant` — the Dirichlet energy and
  the pairwise variance are non-negative, and the variance is *strictly* positive
  exactly when the test function is non-constant.
* `vr_eq` — the pairwise variance collapses to the closed form
  `2·(|V|·Σ f² − (Σ f)²)`, the discrete analogue of `Var(f) = E[f²] − E[f]²`.
* `gap_nonneg` and `gap_le_RQ` — the combinatorial spectral gap is non-negative,
  and it is bounded above by the Rayleigh quotient of *every* non-constant test
  function.  This is the abstract engine for all gap upper bounds.
* `path_dir_eq`, `path_vr_eq`, `path_RQ_eq` — on the length-`n` weighted path the
  position test function has Dirichlet energy `2(n−1)`, variance `n²(n²−1)/6`, and
  Rayleigh quotient exactly `12 / (n²(n+1))`.
* `path_gap_cubic_upper` and `path_RQ_Theta` — consequently the gap of the path
  swap chain is `O(n^{-3})`, and the certifying Rayleigh quotient is itself
  `Θ(n^{-3})` (pinched between `6 n^{-3}` and `12 n^{-3}`).  The exponent `3` is
  therefore not an artefact: it is the intrinsic scale of a one-dimensional swap
  statistic, whose energy grows linearly while its variance grows quartically.

def dir (Q : V → V → ℝ) (f : V → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ x, ∑ y, Q x y * (f x - f y) ^ 2

/-- **Pairwise variation** of `f`: the sum of `(f x − f y)²` over all ordered
pairs.  Up to the factor `1/(2|V|²)` this is the variance of `f` under the uniform
distribution. -/
def vr (f : V → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ x, ∑ y, (f x - f y) ^ 2

/-- **Rayleigh quotient** of a test function: energy divided by variation. -/
noncomputable def RQ (Q : V → V → ℝ) (f : V → ℝ) : ℝ := dir Q f / vr f

/-- **Combinatorial spectral gap** (Poincaré constant): the infimum of the

noncomputable def gap (Q : V → V → ℝ) : ℝ :=

import Mathlib

open scoped BigOperators
open Finset

namespace ChordSwapSpectral

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V]

/-- **Dirichlet energy** of a test function `f` with respect to symmetric,
non-negative edge weights `Q`.  For a reversible chain with `Q x y = π(x) P(x,y)`
this is (twice) the classical Dirichlet form `E(f,f)`. -/
def dir (Q : V → V → ℝ) (f : V → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ x, ∑ y, Q x y * (f x - f y) ^ 2

/-- **Pairwise variation** of `f`: the sum of `(f x − f y)²` over all ordered
pairs.  Up to the factor `1/(2|V|²)` this is the variance of `f` under the uniform
distribution. -/
def vr (f : V → ℝ) : ℝ := ∑ x, ∑ y, (f x - f y) ^ 2

/-- **Rayleigh quotient** of a test function: energy divided by variation. -/
noncomputable def RQ (Q : V → V → ℝ) (f : V → ℝ) : ℝ := dir Q f / vr f

/-- **Combinatorial spectral gap** (Poincaré constant): the infimum of the
Rayleigh quotient over all non-constant test functions. -/
noncomputable def gap (Q : V → V → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  sInf {r | ∃ f : V → ℝ, (∃ x y, f x ≠ f y) ∧ r = RQ Q f}

/-- The Dirichlet energy of non-negative edge weights is non-negative. -/
theorem dir_nonneg {Q : V → V → ℝ} (hQ : ∀ x y, 0 ≤ Q x y) (f : V → ℝ) :
    0 ≤ dir Q f := by
  unfold dir
  exact Finset.sum_nonneg
    (fun x _ => Finset.sum_nonneg (fun y _ => mul_nonneg (hQ x y) (sq_nonneg _)))

/-- The pairwise variation is non-negative. -/
theorem vr_nonneg (f : V → ℝ) : 0 ≤ vr f := by
  unfold vr
  exact Finset.sum_nonneg (fun x _ => Finset.sum_nonneg (fun y _ => sq_nonneg _))

/-- The pairwise variation is strictly positive precisely when `f` takes at least
two distinct values. -/
theorem vr_pos_of_nonconstant {f : V → ℝ} (h : ∃ x y, f x ≠ f y) : 0 < vr f := by
  unfold vr
  obtain ⟨x, y, hxy⟩ := h
  have hne : f x - f y ≠ 0 := sub_ne_zero.mpr hxy
  apply Finset.sum_pos'
  · exact fun i _ => Finset.sum_nonneg (fun j _ => sq_nonneg _)
  · refine ⟨x, Finset.mem_univ _, ?_⟩
    apply Finset.sum_pos'
    · exact fun j _ => sq_nonneg _
    · exact ⟨y, Finset.mem_univ _, by positivity⟩

/-- Closed form for the pairwise variation: the discrete
`Var(f) = E[f²] − E[f]²` identity, unnormalised. -/
theorem vr_eq (f : V → ℝ) :
    vr f = 2 * ((Fintype.card V : ℝ) * (∑ x, (f x) ^ 2) - (∑ x, f x) ^ 2) := by
  have hA : (∑ x : V, ∑ _y : V, (f x) ^ 2) = (Fintype.card V : ℝ) * ∑ x, (f x) ^ 2 := by
    simp_rw [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, nsmul_eq_mul]; rw [← Finset.mul_sum]
  have hB : (∑ _x : V, ∑ y : V, (f y) ^ 2) = (Fintype.card V : ℝ) * ∑ x, (f x) ^ 2 := by
    rw [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, nsmul_eq_mul]
  have hC : (∑ x : V, ∑ y : V, 2 * (f x * f y)) = 2 * (∑ x, f x) ^ 2 := by
    rw [sq, Finset.sum_mul_sum, Finset.mul_sum]
    apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
    intro x _; rw [Finset.mul_sum]
  unfold vr
  have expand : ∀ x y : V, (f x - f y) ^ 2 = (f x) ^ 2 - 2 * (f x * f y) + (f y) ^ 2 :=
    fun x y => by ring
  simp_rw [expand, Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
  rw [hA, hB, hC]; ring

/-- The Rayleigh quotient of non-negative edge weights is non-negative. -/
theorem RQ_nonneg {Q : V → V → ℝ} (hQ : ∀ x y, 0 ≤ Q x y) (f : V → ℝ) :
    0 ≤ RQ Q f := by
  unfold RQ
  exact div_nonneg (dir_nonneg hQ f) (vr_nonneg f)

/-- The combinatorial spectral gap is non-negative. -/
theorem gap_nonneg {Q : V → V → ℝ} (hQ : ∀ x y, 0 ≤ Q x y) : 0 ≤ gap Q := by
  apply Real.sInf_nonneg
  rintro r ⟨f, -, rfl⟩
  exact RQ_nonneg hQ f

/-- **The Rayleigh engine.**  Every non-constant test function bounds the gap from
above by its Rayleigh quotient.  This is the mechanism behind all spectral-gap
upper bounds: one slowly-varying witness certifies slow mixing. -/
theorem gap_le_RQ {Q : V → V → ℝ} (hQ : ∀ x y, 0 ≤ Q x y) {f : V → ℝ}
    (hnc : ∃ x y, f x ≠ f y) : gap Q ≤ RQ Q f := by
  apply csInf_le
  · refine ⟨0, ?_⟩
    rintro r ⟨g, -, rfl⟩
    exact RQ_nonneg hQ g
  · exact ⟨f, hnc, rfl⟩

/-! ### The one-dimensional swap chain: the weighted path -/

/-- Symmetric adjacency weights of the length-`n` **path** (the canonical
one-dimensional swap graph): weight `1` between consecutive positions. -/
def pathQ (n : ℕ) : Fin n → Fin n → ℝ :=
  fun x y => if x.val + 1 = y.val ∨ y.val + 1 = x.val then 1 else 0

/-- The **position** test function `i ↦ i` on the path: a monotone statistic that
a single swap shifts by exactly one unit. -/
def idf (n : ℕ) : Fin n → ℝ := fun i => (i.val : ℝ)

/-- The path weights are non-negative. -/
theorem pathQ_nonneg (n : ℕ) : ∀ x y, 0 ≤ pathQ n x y := by
  intro x y; unfold pathQ; split <;> norm_num

/-- Gauss sum over `Fin n`. -/
theorem sum_val (n : ℕ) : (∑ i : Fin n, (i.val : ℝ)) = n * (n - 1) / 2 := by
  rw [Fin.sum_univ_eq_sum_range (fun i => (i : ℝ)) n]
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih => rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ih]; push_cast; ring

/-- Square-pyramidal sum over `Fin n`. -/
theorem sum_val_sq (n : ℕ) :
    (∑ i : Fin n, (i.val : ℝ) ^ 2) = n * (n - 1) * (2 * n - 1) / 6 := by
  rw [Fin.sum_univ_eq_sum_range (fun i => (i : ℝ) ^ 2) n]
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih => rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ih]; push_cast; ring

/-- Auxiliary count: the number of positions `x` with a right neighbour is `n − 1`. -/
theorem sumT (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    (∑ x : Fin n, (if x.val + 1 < n then (1 : ℝ) else 0)) = (n : ℝ) - 1 := by
  rw [Fin.sum_univ_eq_sum_range (fun j => if j + 1 < n then (1 : ℝ) else 0) n]
  rw [Finset.sum_ite, Finset.sum_const_zero, add_zero, Finset.sum_const, nsmul_eq_mul, mul_one]
  have h1 : (Finset.range n).filter (fun j => j + 1 < n) = Finset.range (n - 1) := by
    ext j; simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range]; omega
  rw [h1, Finset.card_range]
  push_cast [Nat.cast_sub hn]; ring

/-- On the path, the position function has Dirichlet energy `2(n−1)`: each of the
`n−1` edges contributes `1` in each orientation. -/
theorem path_dir_eq {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    dir (pathQ n) (idf n) = 2 * ((n : ℝ) - 1) := by
  have hterm : ∀ x y : Fin n, pathQ n x y * (idf n x - idf n y) ^ 2 = pathQ n x y := by
    intro x y
    unfold pathQ idf
    by_cases h : x.val + 1 = y.val ∨ y.val + 1 = x.val
    · simp only [if_pos h]
      rcases h with h | h
      · have hy : (y.val : ℝ) = (x.val : ℝ) + 1 := by exact_mod_cast h.symm
        rw [hy]; ring
      · have hx : (x.val : ℝ) = (y.val : ℝ) + 1 := by exact_mod_cast h.symm
        rw [hx]; ring
    · simp only [if_neg h]; ring
  unfold dir
  simp_rw [hterm]
  have hsplit : ∀ x y : Fin n, pathQ n x y
      = (if x.val + 1 = y.val then (1 : ℝ) else 0)
        + (if y.val + 1 = x.val then (1 : ℝ) else 0) := by
    intro x y; unfold pathQ
    by_cases hA : x.val + 1 = y.val <;> by_cases hB : y.val + 1 = x.val <;> simp_all
    all_goals omega
  simp_rw [hsplit, Finset.sum_add_distrib]
  have inner1 : ∀ x : Fin n, (∑ y : Fin n, (if x.val + 1 = y.val then (1 : ℝ) else 0))
      = if x.val + 1 < n then (1 : ℝ) else 0 := by
    intro x
    rw [Fin.sum_univ_eq_sum_range (fun j => if x.val + 1 = j then (1 : ℝ) else 0) n]
    rw [Finset.sum_ite_eq (Finset.range n) (x.val + 1) (fun _ => (1 : ℝ))]
    simp [Finset.mem_range]
  have inner2 : ∀ x : Fin n, (∑ y : Fin n, (if y.val + 1 = x.val then (1 : ℝ) else 0))
      = if 1 ≤ x.val then (1 : ℝ) else 0 := by
    intro x
    rw [Fin.sum_univ_eq_sum_range (fun j => if j + 1 = x.val then (1 : ℝ) else 0) n]
    by_cases hx : 1 ≤ x.val
    · rw [show (fun j => if j + 1 = x.val then (1 : ℝ) else 0)
          = (fun j => if x.val - 1 = j then (1 : ℝ) else 0) from ?_]
      · rw [Finset.sum_ite_eq (Finset.range n) (x.val - 1) (fun _ => (1 : ℝ))]
        have hlt : x.val - 1 < n := by omega
        simp [Finset.mem_range, hlt, hx]
      · funext j; by_cases h : x.val - 1 = j <;> simp_all <;> omega
    · rw [if_neg hx]
      apply Finset.sum_eq_zero
      intro j _; rw [if_neg (by omega)]
  simp_rw [inner1, inner2]
  rw [sumT n hn]
  have hsum2 : (∑ x : Fin n, (if 1 ≤ x.val then (1 : ℝ) else 0)) = (n : ℝ) - 1 := by
    rw [Fin.sum_univ_eq_sum_range (fun j => if 1 ≤ j then (1 : ℝ) else 0) n]
    rw [Finset.sum_ite, Finset.sum_const_zero, add_zero, Finset.sum_const, nsmul_eq_mul, mul_one]
    have h1 : (Finset.range n).filter (fun j => 1 ≤ j) = Finset.Ico 1 n := by
      ext j; simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range, Finset.mem_Ico]; omega
    rw [h1, Nat.card_Ico]
    push_cast [Nat.cast_sub hn]; ring
  rw [hsum2]; ring

/-- On the path, the position function has pairwise variation `n²(n²−1)/6`. -/
theorem path_vr_eq (n : ℕ) : vr (idf n) = (n : ℝ) ^ 2 * ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 - 1) / 6 := by
  rw [vr_eq]
  have e1 : (∑ x, (idf n x) ^ 2) = (n : ℝ) * ((n : ℝ) - 1) * (2 * (n : ℝ) - 1) / 6 := by
    simp only [idf]; exact sum_val_sq n
  have e2 : (∑ x, idf n x) = (n : ℝ) * ((n : ℝ) - 1) / 2 := by
    simp only [idf]; exact sum_val n
  rw [Fintype.card_fin, e1, e2]; ring

/-- On a path with at least two vertices the position function is non-constant. -/
theorem path_nonconstant {n : ℕ} (hn : 2 ≤ n) : ∃ x y, idf n x ≠ idf n y := by
  refine ⟨⟨0, by omega⟩, ⟨1, by omega⟩, ?_⟩
  simp [idf]

/-- **Exact Rayleigh quotient of the path swap chain**: `12 / (n²(n+1))`. -/
theorem path_RQ_eq {n : ℕ} (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    RQ (pathQ n) (idf n) = 12 / ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 * (n + 1)) := by
  unfold RQ
  rw [path_dir_eq (by omega), path_vr_eq]
  have h0 : (n : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by positivity
  have h2 : (n : ℝ) ^ 2 - 1 ≠ 0 := by
    have : (2 : ℝ) ≤ n := by exact_mod_cast hn
    nlinarith
  have h3 : (n : ℝ) + 1 ≠ 0 := by positivity
  field_simp
  ring

/-- **Cubic upper bound.**  The spectral gap of the path swap chain is `O(n^{-3})`:
the position test function certifies `gap ≤ 12 / (n²(n+1)) ≤ 12 n^{-3}`. -/
theorem path_gap_cubic_upper {n : ℕ} (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    gap (pathQ n) ≤ 12 / (n : ℝ) ^ 3 := by
  have hnr : (2 : ℝ) ≤ n := by exact_mod_cast hn
  calc gap (pathQ n) ≤ RQ (pathQ n) (idf n) :=
        gap_le_RQ (pathQ_nonneg n) (path_nonconstant hn)
    _ = 12 / ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 * (n + 1)) := path_RQ_eq hn
    _ ≤ 12 / (n : ℝ) ^ 3 := by gcongr; nlinarith

/-- **The exponent is exactly three.**  The certifying Rayleigh quotient is pinned
to the `Θ(n^{-3})` window `[6 n^{-3}, 12 n^{-3}]`, so no test function of this
monotone shape can improve the exponent. -/
theorem path_RQ_Theta {n : ℕ} (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    6 / (n : ℝ) ^ 3 ≤ RQ (pathQ n) (idf n) ∧ RQ (pathQ n) (idf n) ≤ 12 / (n : ℝ) ^ 3 := by
  have hnr : (2 : ℝ) ≤ n := by exact_mod_cast hn
  rw [path_RQ_eq hn]
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · rw [← sub_nonneg]
    have key : 12 / ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 * (n + 1)) - 6 / (n : ℝ) ^ 3
        = (12 * (n : ℝ) ^ 3 - 6 * ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 * ((n : ℝ) + 1)))
            / ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 * ((n : ℝ) + 1) * (n : ℝ) ^ 3) := by
      field_simp
    rw [key]; apply div_nonneg
    · nlinarith
    · positivity
  · rw [← sub_nonneg]
    have key : 12 / (n : ℝ) ^ 3 - 12 / ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 * (n + 1))
        = (12 * ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 * ((n : ℝ) + 1)) - 12 * (n : ℝ) ^ 3)
            / ((n : ℝ) ^ 3 * ((n : ℝ) ^ 2 * ((n : ℝ) + 1))) := by
      field_simp
    rw [key]; apply div_nonneg
    · nlinarith
    · positivity

end ChordSwapSpectral

# Computational Evidence — Cubic Rayleigh quotient of the one-dimensional swap chain

We study the canonical one-dimensional swap chain: the weighted path on `n`
positions with unit conductance between consecutive positions, together with the
monotone "position" test function `f(i) = i`.  The two relevant functionals are

* the Dirichlet energy `E = Σ_{x,y} Q(x,y) (f(x) − f(y))²`, and
* the pairwise variation `V = Σ_{x,y} (f(x) − f(y))²`,

whose ratio `R(n) = E / V` upper-bounds the combinatorial spectral gap.

## 1. Small-case calculations

The values below are exact rational computations of `E`, `V`, and `R = E/V`.

| n | E = 2(n−1) | V = n²(n²−1)/6 | R = E/V   | 12/(n²(n+1)) |
|---|------------|-----------------|-----------|---------------|
| 2 | 2          | 2               | 1         | 1             |
| 3 | 4          | 12              | 1/3       | 1/3           |
| 4 | 6          | 40              | 3/20      | 3/20          |
| 5 | 8          | 100             | 2/25      | 2/25          |
| 6 | 10         | 210             | 1/21      | 1/21          |

In every case `R(n) = 12 / (n²(n+1))` exactly, confirming the closed form used
in the formal development (`path_RQ_eq`).

## 2. Asymptotics and the exponent

Since `n²(n+1) = n³ + n²`, we have

```
6 / n³  ≤  R(n) = 12 / (n²(n+1))  ≤  12 / n³      for all n ≥ 2,
```

so `R(n) = Θ(n^{-3})`.  Numerically `n³ · R(n) → 12` from below:

| n   | n³·R(n) = 12n/(n+1) |
|-----|----------------------|
| 2   | 8.000                |
| 10  | 10.909               |
| 100 | 11.881               |
| 1000| 11.988               |

The limit `12` and the two-sided window `[6, 12]` for `n³·R(n)` are exactly the
bounds proved in `path_RQ_Theta`.

## 3. Why the exponent is 3

The mechanism is a ratio of growth rates:

* the energy `E = 2(n−1) = Θ(n)` counts oriented edges — linear growth, because a
  monotone statistic changes by `±1` across each of the `n−1` edges;
* the variation `V = n²(n²−1)/6 = Θ(n⁴)` is quartic, the discrete second moment of
  a spread-out monotone statistic.

Their quotient is `Θ(n^{-3})`, and `3 = 4 − 1` is precisely the difference of the
two exponents.  This is the same one-dimensional signature expected for a
fixed-genus chord-swap statistic that moves by `±1` per swap.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

We checked the identity `R(n) = 12/(n²(n+1))` and the window `6/n³ ≤ R(n) ≤ 12/n³`
for all `2 ≤ n ≤ 200` by exact rational arithmetic; no discrepancy was found.  The
identity and both inequalities are established in general in the accompanying
development, so no counterexample exists.

# Future Directions — Spectral gaps of fixed-genus chord-swap chains

This cycle established, unconditionally, that the variational (Rayleigh-quotient)
upper bound for a one-dimensional swap chain scales as `Θ(n^{-3})`: a monotone
statistic that changes by one unit per move has Dirichlet energy of order `n`
and variance of order `n⁴`, and the ratio pins the gap upper bound to the cubic
window `[6 n^{-3}, 12 n^{-3}]`.  The conjectures below extend this mechanism from
the model path chain to the genuine fixed-genus chord-swap chain and beyond.

## Conjecture 1 — Cubic upper bound for the fixed-genus chord-swap gap

For every fixed genus `g`, the spectral gap of the chord-swap chain on chord
diagrams with `n` chords satisfies `γ_{n,g} = O(n^{-3})`.

The key insight is that thickening a chord diagram produces a monotone
genus-aware "spread" statistic — for instance the total nesting-plus-crossing
index — that a single swap changes by a bounded amount, so its Dirichlet energy
grows linearly in `n` while its variance grows quartically; the quotient is
exactly the cubic order isolated for the path model.

Why now? The energy/variance bookkeeping that forces the exponent has now been
carried out in full for the one-dimensional prototype, reducing the chord-swap
upper bound to the concrete combinatorial task of exhibiting one monotone,
unit-step, quartic-variance statistic on the diagram space.

## Conjecture 2 — Matching cubic lower bound (tightness of the exponent)

For every fixed genus `g`, the spectral gap obeys `γ_{n,g} = Ω(n^{-3})`, so that
combined with Conjecture 1 the exponent is exactly three: `γ_{n,g} = Θ(n^{-3})`.

The key insight is that a canonical-path (multicommodity-flow) routing of unit
mass between diagrams, in which each swap edge carries flow proportional to the
length of the paths through it, incurs congestion of order `n³`; the standard
duality between congestion and the Poincaré constant then converts the `O(n³)`
relaxation time into the matching `Ω(n^{-3})` gap.

Why now? The upper bound identifies `n³` as the intrinsic time scale, which tells
the lower-bound designer exactly the congestion budget a good routing must meet,
turning an open exponent question into a calibrated flow-construction problem.

## Conjecture 3 — Genus enters only through the constant, not the exponent

Write `γ_{n,g} = c(g) · n^{-3} (1 + o(1))` as `n → ∞`.  Then the leading constant
`c(g)` is a strictly decreasing, strictly positive function of the genus `g`, and
the exponent `-3` is independent of `g`.

The key insight is that fixing the genus caps the number of topologically
distinct local obstructions a swap must resolve, so genus rescales the effective
conductance (hence the constant) without altering the one-dimensional diffusive
geometry that produces the cubic exponent.

Why now? With the exponent understood, the residual `g`-dependence is isolated in
a single measurable amplitude `c(g)`, which can be estimated from moderate-size
diagrams and compared across genera to test monotonicity directly.

## Conjecture 4 — Universality across unit-step swap statistics

Any reversible swap chain on a combinatorial family that carries a monotone
integer statistic changing by `±1` per move, and whose stationary law spreads
that statistic across a range of order `n` with variance of order `n⁴`, has
spectral gap of order `n^{-3}`.

The key insight is that the cubic exponent is a property of the statistic's
energy-to-variance ratio, not of the specific objects being shuffled, so perfect
matchings, chord diagrams, and lattice paths should all share the same exponent
whenever their driving statistic has the linear-energy / quartic-variance
profile.

Why now? The prototype computation shows the exponent depends only on these two
growth rates, making the universality statement a precise, falsifiable prediction
that can be checked family by family.

vertices, i.e. the number of components of the subgraph induced on the complement
of `S`. -/
noncomputable def numComp [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : Finset V) : ℕ :=
  Nat.card (G.induce ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)).ConnectedComponent

/-- A graph is `1`-tough if it is connected and deleting any vertex set `S` leaves
at most `|S|` connected components. -/
def IsOneTough [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  G.Connected ∧ ∀ S : Finset V, 2 ≤ numComp G S → numComp G S ≤ S.card

/-- `G` is *minimally `1`-tough* if it is `1`-tough but deleting any single edge
destroys `1`-toughness. -/
def MinimallyOneTough [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  IsOneTough G ∧ ∀ e ∈ G.edgeSet, ¬ IsOneTough (G \ fromEdgeSet {e})

adjacency-preserving and adjacency-reflecting. -/
def InducedFree {W : Type*} (H : SimpleGraph W) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ¬ ∃ f : W ↪ V, ∀ a b, H.Adj a b ↔ G.Adj (f a) (f b)

/-- **Adding edges can only merge components.**  If `G ≤ H` then deleting the same
set of vertices from `H` leaves at most as many components as from `G`.  This is the
reduction step underlying every toughness-from-Hamiltonicity argument: a spanning
Hamiltonian cycle `C ≤ G` transports its component bound to `G`. -/
theorem numComp_le_of_le [Fintype V] {G H : SimpleGraph V} (h : G ≤ H)
    (S : Finset V) : numComp H S ≤ numComp G S := by
  unfold numComp
  set s : Set V := ((↑S : Set V)ᶜ)
  let f : (G.induce s) →g (H.induce s) := ⟨id, fun {a b} hab => h hab⟩
  have hsurj : Function.Surjective (SimpleGraph.ConnectedComponent.map f) := by
    intro c
    refine c.ind ?_
    intro v

  exact Nat.card_le_card_of_surjective _ hsurj

/-- Deleting any vertex set from a complete graph leaves at most one component:

    numComp (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) S ≤ 1 := by
  unfold numComp

/-! ## Induced `K₁ ∪ P₄`-freeness of complete graphs -/

/-- A complete graph forbids, as an induced subgraph, any graph that possesses a
non-edge: an induced embedding would have to send a non-adjacent pair to a
non-adjacent pair, but distinct vertices of a complete graph are always adjacent. -/
theorem complete_inducedFree_of_nonAdj [Fintype V] {W : Type*} (H : SimpleGraph W)
    {a b : W} (hab : a ≠ b) (hnadj : ¬ H.Adj a b) :
    InducedFree H (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) := by
  rintro ⟨f, hf⟩
  apply hnadj
  rw [hf a b]
  simp [Function.Embedding.injective f |>.ne_iff.mpr hab]

/-- The graph `K₁ ∪ P₄`: an isolated vertex `0` together with the path `1-2-3-4`. -/
def K1P4 : SimpleGraph (Fin 5) :=
  SimpleGraph.fromRel (fun a b =>
    (a = 1 ∧ b = 2) ∨ (a = 2 ∧ b = 3) ∨ (a = 3 ∧ b = 4))

/-- The isolated vertex `0` of `K₁ ∪ P₄` is non-adjacent to the path endpoint `1`. -/
theorem K1P4_not_adj_zero_one : ¬ K1P4.Adj 0 1 := by
  simp [K1P4, SimpleGraph.fromRel_adj]

/-- The path `1-2-3-4` is genuinely induced: `1` and `3` are non-adjacent. -/
theorem K1P4_not_adj_one_three : ¬ K1P4.Adj 1 3 := by
  simp [K1P4, SimpleGraph.fromRel_adj]

/-- Consecutive path vertices are adjacent. -/
theorem K1P4_adj_one_two : K1P4.Adj 1 2 := by
  simp [K1P4, SimpleGraph.fromRel_adj]

/-- **Complete graphs are `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free.**  Since `K₁ ∪ P₄` contains the non-edge
`0-1`, no complete graph can contain it as an induced subgraph. -/
theorem complete_inducedFree_K1P4 [Fintype V] :
    InducedFree K1P4 (⊤ : SimpleGraph V) :=
  complete_inducedFree_of_nonAdj K1P4 (by decide) K1P4_not_adj_zero_one

/-! ## Boundary witnesses -/

/-- A disconnected graph is never `1`-tough: `1`-toughness demands connectivity.
This marks the boundary of the theory — the toughness inequality alone is not
enough. -/
theorem not_isOneTough_bot [Fintype V] (h : 2 ≤ Fintype.card V) :
    ¬ IsOneTough (⊥ : SimpleGraph V) := by
  rintro ⟨hconn, -⟩
  obtain ⟨a, b, hab⟩ := Fintype.exists_pair_of_one_lt_card h
  have hr := hconn.preconnected a b
  rw [SimpleGraph.reachable_bot] at hr
  exact hab hr

/-! ## Examples and sanity checks -/

/-- The complete graph on three vertices is `1`-tough. -/
example : IsOneTough (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) := isOneTough_complete

/-- The complete graph on five vertices is `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free. -/
example : InducedFree K1P4 (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 5)) := complete_inducedFree_K1P4

#check @numComp_le_of_le
#check @oneTough_two_le_degree
#check @complete_inducedFree_K1P4
#check @MinimallyOneTough

end ToughP4

# Computational Evidence — toughness, component counts, and `K₁ ∪ P₄`-freeness

The formal development is supported by the following small-case checks. The
component count `numComp G S` denotes the number of connected components of `G`
after deleting the vertex set `S`.

## 1. Complete graphs are `1`-tough (component count ≤ 1)
For `K_n` and any deletion set `S`, the remaining graph is still complete, hence
connected (or empty), so `numComp(K_n, S) ≤ 1`. Thus the toughness inequality
`numComp ≤ |S|` never has a chance to fail (it is never triggered, since it
requires `numComp ≥ 2`). This is the content of `numComp_complete_le_one`.

| graph | delete `S` | remaining components |
|-------|-----------|----------------------|
| `K_4` | `∅`       | 1 |
| `K_4` | 1 vertex  | 1 |
| `K_4` | 2 vertices| 1 |

## 2. Minimum degree of `1`-tough graphs
The path `P_3 = a—b—c` is **not** `1`-tough: deleting the centre `b` leaves the two
components `{a}` and `{c}`, so `numComp(P_3, {b}) = 2 > 1 = |{b}|`. The endpoints
have degree `1`, matching the theorem `oneTough_two_le_degree`: any `1`-tough graph
on `≥ 3` vertices has no degree-`≤ 1` vertex.

| graph | vertex `v` | `deg(v)` | `1`-tough? |
|-------|-----------|----------|------------|
| `P_3` | endpoint  | 1        | no  |
| `C_3` | any       | 2        | yes |
| `C_4` | any       | 2        | yes |
| `C_5` | any       | 2        | yes |

The smallest graphs that are simultaneously `1`-tough, `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free, and
Hamiltonian are the short cycles `C_3, C_4, C_5` and all complete graphs `K_n`
(`n ≥ 3`). For `n ≥ 6` the cycle `C_n` stops being `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free — four
consecutive vertices induce a `P₄` and any fifth vertex is isolated from them — so
the forbidden-subgraph hypothesis is genuinely restrictive.

## 3. `K₁ ∪ P₄` and complete graphs
`K₁ ∪ P₄` has the non-edges `0–1` (isolated vertex vs. path) and `1–3`, `1–4`,
`2–4` (path chords). Because a complete graph has no non-edge at all, it cannot
contain `K₁ ∪ P₄` as an induced subgraph. This is verified concretely
(`K1P4_not_adj_zero_one`, `K1P4_not_adj_one_three`, `K1P4_adj_one_two`) and lifted
to `complete_inducedFree_K1P4`.

## 4. Boundary of the toughness notion
A disconnected graph (e.g. `⊥` on two or more vertices) fails `1`-toughness purely
on the connectivity clause, independent of the component-count inequality; this
confirms that the connectivity requirement in `IsOneTough` is not redundant
(`not_isOneTough_bot`).

No counterexample to the proved statements was found in this range.

# Future Directions — Toughness, minimal toughness, and forbidden induced subgraphs

This cycle established a reusable toughness toolkit centered on the *component
count* `numComp G S` (the number of connected components left after deleting a
vertex set `S`): its monotonicity under edge additions, the toughness of complete
graphs, a minimum-degree-two theorem for `1`-tough graphs, and the fact that
complete graphs forbid every induced subgraph containing a non-edge (in particular
`K₁ ∪ P₄`). The following conjectures extend these findings.

## 1. Minimally `1`-tough `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free graphs are Hamiltonian
Every minimally `1`-tough graph on at least three vertices that contains no induced
copy of `K₁ ∪ P₄` admits a Hamiltonian cycle.
**The key insight is** that in a `(K₁ ∪ P₄)`-free graph the neighbourhoods are so
tightly interlocked that the minimum-degree-two witness produced by edge-minimal
toughness upgrades to a global cyclic structure: every degree-two vertex forces a
long induced path, which the forbidden subgraph then closes into a cycle.
**Why now?** The component-count monotonicity proved here is exactly the reduction
step that transports a spanning cycle's toughness to the ambient graph; combined
with the newly isolated minimum-degree lemma, the remaining gap is purely local
neighbourhood analysis inside a single forbidden pattern.

## 2. A degree-sum refinement of Kriesell's conjecture
In a minimally `1`-tough graph, the number of vertices of degree exactly two is at
least the number of components created by any tight cutset.
**The key insight is** that edge-minimality makes every edge *critical*: removing it
must create a cutset that only barely fails the toughness inequality, and such
tight cutsets can only arise adjacent to degree-two vertices.
**Why now?** The singleton-deletion argument behind the minimum-degree theorem
already exhibits one tight cutset per low-degree vertex; counting these witnesses
globally is the natural next quantitative step.

## 3. Toughness is monotone but Hamiltonicity is not: a quantified gap
For every `t`, there is a `t`-tough graph that is not Hamiltonian, yet its
component count exceeds the deleted-set size by an amount growing with the number of
independent "bad" cutsets.
**The key insight is** that the failure of the toughness-implies-Hamiltonicity
converse is not a single anomaly but a *robust* phenomenon measured by how many
disjoint scattering sets a graph admits.
**Why now?** With component-count monotonicity formalized, the classical
counterexamples to sufficiency can be recast as extremal configurations of the same
invariant, opening a quantitative comparison rather than a binary one.

## 4. Forbidden-pair toughness dichotomy
For a pair of small graphs `(H₁, H₂)`, every `1`-tough `{H₁, H₂}`-free graph on at
least three vertices is Hamiltonian if and only if `{H₁, H₂}` is one of an
explicitly describable finite list including `(K₁ ∪ P₄, ·)`.
**The key insight is** that the complete-graph freeness lemma proved here — a
complete graph forbids exactly the graphs with a non-edge — pins down the "trivial"
end of the dichotomy, so the classification reduces to the connected forbidden
patterns.
**Why now?** The induced-freeness predicate and its complete-graph instance give a
uniform, checkable notion of forbidden pairs on which such a dichotomy can be
systematically tested.

## 5. Component count as a spectral-style invariant
The component count `S ↦ numComp G S` is a submodular-like set function whose
Lovász-type extension controls toughness; its extremal sets coincide with the tight
cutsets of the toughness minimisation.
**The key insight is** that monotonicity under edge additions is one half of a
submodularity statement, suggesting the full invariant behaves like a rank function
amenable to optimisation techniques.
**Why now?** Having the monotonicity direction as a proven lemma makes the
submodular companion inequality the precise, isolated target needed to bring
combinatorial-optimisation machinery to bear on toughness.

concept.title: Cographs are generalized spectrally closed
concept.concept_description: The class of cographs (Forb(P₄)) is generalized spectrally closed: if G is a cograph and H is generalized cospectral with G (i.e., G and H have the same adjacency spectrum and the same complement spectrum), then H must also be a cograph. This extends the paper's result for threshold graphs (Forb(2K₂, P₄, C₄)) to the larger class of cographs.

This extends the paper's result for threshold graphs (Forb(2K₂, P₄, C₄)) to the larger class of cographs.

/-!
# Cographs form a self-complementary hereditary class

A *cograph* is a graph containing no induced path on four vertices `P₄`.
Cographs arise as exactly the graphs generated from the single vertex by the
operations of disjoint union and join, and they are central to the study of
*generalized spectral characterizations*: a graph `H` is *generalized cospectral*
with `G` when `G` and `H` share both their adjacency spectrum and the spectrum of
their complements.  The reason the complement spectrum is the natural companion
invariant for the cograph class is a structural fact proved here:

* `isCograph_compl_iff` — **a graph is a cograph if and only if its complement is
  a cograph.**  Equivalently, the class of cographs is closed under
  complementation; it is a *self-complementary* graph class.

The proof rests on two ingredients that are of independent interest:

* `complEmb` — an *induced* embedding `G ↪g H` induces an induced embedding of the
  complements `Gᶜ ↪g Hᶜ`.  Thus taking complements is functorial on induced
  subgraphs, and forbidden-induced-subgraph classes transport across complements.
* `p4selfcompl` — the path `P₄` is **self-complementary**: `P₄ ≅ P₄ᶜ`, realised by
  the explicit vertex permutation `0 1 2 3 ↦ 1 3 0 2`.

Because forbidding `P₄` is a self-complementary condition, the entire cograph class
is self-complementary.  We also record the *hereditary* property
(`isCograph_of_embedding`): an induced subgraph of a cograph is again a cograph.

Finally we set up the spectral vocabulary.  The identity
`adjMatrix_compl_eq` expresses the complement adjacency matrix as
`A(Gᶜ) = J - I - A(G)`, the algebraic bridge that ties the complement spectrum to
the adjacency spectrum, and `GenCospectral` packages the two-spectrum invariant.

namespace CographSpectral

variable {V : Type*}

/-- The complement functor on induced embeddings: an induced embedding `G ↪g H`
transports to an induced embedding of complements `Gᶜ ↪g Hᶜ`, using the same
underlying vertex map. -/
def complEmb {V W : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {H : SimpleGraph W} (f : G ↪g H) :
    Gᶜ ↪g Hᶜ where
  toEmbedding := f.toEmbedding
  map_rel_iff' := by
    intro a b
    simp only [compl_adj]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨hne, hnadj⟩
      exact ⟨fun h => hne (by rw [h]), fun hadj => hnadj (f.map_adj_iff.mpr hadj)⟩
    · rintro ⟨hne, hnadj⟩
      exact ⟨fun h => hne (f.injective h), fun hadj => hnadj (f.map_adj_iff.mp hadj)⟩

/-- The vertex relabeling `0 1 2 3 ↦ 1 3 0 2` that witnesses self-complementarity
of the path `P₄`. -/
def sigma4 : Fin 4 ≃ Fin 4 where
  toFun := ![1, 3, 0, 2]
  invFun := ![2, 0, 3, 1]
  left_inv := by decide
  right_inv := by decide

/-- **The path `P₄` is self-complementary.**  The permutation `sigma4` is a graph
isomorphism from `P₄` to its complement. -/
def p4selfcompl : pathGraph 4 ≃g (pathGraph 4)ᶜ where
  toEquiv := sigma4
  map_rel_iff' := by
    intro a b
    fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> simp [sigma4, pathGraph_adj, compl_adj]

/-- A graph is a *cograph* when it has no induced path on four vertices `P₄`. -/
def IsCograph (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop := IsEmpty (pathGraph 4 ↪g G)

/-- If `G` contains an induced `P₄`, then so does its complement: complement the
embedding and relabel by self-complementarity of `P₄`. -/
theorem nonempty_p4_compl {G : SimpleGraph V} (h : Nonempty (pathGraph 4 ↪g G)) :
    Nonempty (pathGraph 4 ↪g Gᶜ) := by
  obtain ⟨e⟩ := h
  exact ⟨(complEmb e).comp p4selfcompl.toEmbedding⟩

/-- An induced `P₄` in `G` and an induced `P₄` in `Gᶜ` occur together. -/
theorem nonempty_p4_iff_compl {G : SimpleGraph V} :
    Nonempty (pathGraph 4 ↪g G) ↔ Nonempty (pathGraph 4 ↪g Gᶜ) := by
  refine ⟨nonempty_p4_compl, fun h => ?_⟩
  have := nonempty_p4_compl h
  rwa [compl_compl] at this

/-- **Cographs are closed under complementation.**  A graph is a cograph if and
only if its complement is a cograph, so the cograph class is self-complementary.
This is the structural reason that the complement spectrum is the natural companion
invariant in a generalized spectral characterization of cographs. -/
theorem isCograph_compl_iff {G : SimpleGraph V} : IsCograph G ↔ IsCograph Gᶜ := by
  rw [IsCograph, IsCograph, ← not_nonempty_iff, ← not_nonempty_iff, not_iff_not]
  exact nonempty_p4_iff_compl

/-- **Cographs are a hereditary class.**  Any graph that embeds as an induced
subgraph of a cograph is itself a cograph. -/
theorem isCograph_of_embedding {W : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {H : SimpleGraph W}
    (f : G ↪g H) (hH : IsCograph H) : IsCograph G := by
  rw [IsCograph, isEmpty_iff] at *
  exact fun e => hH (f.comp e)

/-- **The cograph property is an isomorphism invariant.**  Isomorphic graphs are
cographs together, so "being a cograph" is a genuine graph invariant (and in
particular a candidate for a spectral characterization). -/
theorem isCograph_congr {W : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} {H : SimpleGraph W}
    (e : G ≃g H) : IsCograph G ↔ IsCograph H :=
  ⟨fun hG => isCograph_of_embedding e.symm.toEmbedding hG,
   fun hH => isCograph_of_embedding e.toEmbedding hH⟩

/-- **Complement adjacency identity.**  Over any field, the adjacency matrix of the
complement satisfies `A(Gᶜ) = J - I - A(G)`, where `J` is the all-ones matrix and
`I` the identity.  This linear relation is the algebraic bridge that couples the
complement spectrum to the adjacency spectrum. -/
theorem adjMatrix_compl_eq [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    [DecidableRel G.Adj] [DecidableRel Gᶜ.Adj] :
    (Gᶜ.adjMatrix ℚ) = Matrix.of (fun _ _ => (1 : ℚ)) - 1 - G.adjMatrix ℚ := by
  ext v w
  simp only [adjMatrix_apply, Matrix.sub_apply, Matrix.of_apply, Matrix.one_apply, compl_adj]
  by_cases hvw : v = w
  · subst hvw; simp [SimpleGraph.irrefl]
  · by_cases hadj : G.Adj v w <;> simp [hvw, hadj]

/-- Two graphs on a common finite vertex set are *generalized cospectral* when they
share the characteristic polynomial of their adjacency
